To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Kv1.1 and Kv7.2 channels localize to the AIS through interactions with the ankyrin G and SAP97 adaptor proteins, and that mutations in the Kv1.1, Kv1.2, Kv7.2, and Nav1.6 channels alter their AIS targeting and localization, and that these mutations are associated with epilepsy.
the Kv1, Kv2 and Kv4 channel subunits, as well as the Nav1.6 channel subunit, are trafficked to the AIS by distinct mechanisms, and that these mechanisms are perturbed in epilepsy.

the AIS localization of Kv4.3 channels is dependent upon the presence of a specific motif (the C-terminus) that is required for binding to a specific adaptor protein (Ankyrin G) and that the AIS localization and trafficking of Kv4 channels is regulated by the activity state and phosphorylation status of the channel.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the trafficking and localization of voltage-gated ion channels in neurons, with an emphasis on those channels found at the axon inital segment (AIS).
understanding the cellular mechanisms that regulate neuronal voltage gated ion channels at the AIS

the trafficking mechanisms that underlie neuronal voltage gated ion channels localization at the AIS, how these trafficking mechanisms are altered in the setting of epilepsy, and how this contributes to the epileptic phenotype.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
trafficking mechanisms underlying neuronal voltage-gated ion channel localization at axon initial segment is not yet clear.
the AIS is the most complex subcellular domain of the neuron, and the mechanisms that govern the localization and trafficking of voltage gated ion channels to the AIS are equally as complex.
trafficking mechanisms underlying AIS localization of Kv and Nav channel subunits is complex and not fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the trafficking of ion channels to the AIS is a complex process that is regulated by many mechanisms including: 1) the intrinsic properties of ion channels, 2) the presence of other ion channels, 3) the presence of scaffolding proteins and 4) the actin cytoskeleton.
trafficking mechanisms are a major contributor to AIS channel localization and that trafficking defects are likely to contribute to epilepsy.
Kv and Nav channel trafficking at the AIS is a dynamic and regulated process, and that trafficking mechanisms are altered in epilepsy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
trafficking of Kv and Na channels to the AIS is complex and involves a variety of mechanisms.
the AIS is not a static structure, but rather is a highly dynamic and regulated structure that is constantly being modified in response to a myriad of stimuli.
Kv channel trafficking to the AIS is mediated by the Kv2 channel auxiliary subunit beta2, while Nav channel trafficking is mediated by the Nav channel auxiliary subunit alpha2delta.
